plan.topic: Plague myths vs facts: 6 beliefs circulating now, each corrected by the agency that answers it
plan.angle: Slide 1: 'Plague: 6 myths vs what CDC and WHO say', with the status line 'As of Oct 10, 2026, WHO: a key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the Irkutsk oblast death (WHO Disease Outbreak News).' Myths: (1) Extinct → CDC's live US wording at publish time ('an average of five human plague cases are reported each year', range 0–17). (2) No cure → CDC: 'Plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly.' (3) Airborne like COVID or measles → CDC: pneumonic plague 'requires direct and close contact'; infected people or animals 'can sometimes cough droplets'. (4) All plague spreads between people → CDC: 'Transmission of these droplets is the only way that plague can spread between people' (CDC How Plague Spreads), with no added absolute in our voice. (5) Home antibiotics protect me → health authorities give close contacts a 7-day preventive course (WHO); don't self-treat or stockpile. (6) Only rats → wild rodents and their fleas, and pets can carry fleas home (CDC); 'follow the label; some dog flea products (e.g. permethrin) are toxic to cats'. Final slide: CDC's 4 pneumonic signs (fever, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain); possible exposure means contact a doctor or local health authority urgently; 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' No bioweapon or lab-leak myths.
plan.working_title: Plague: 6 Myths vs What CDC and WHO Actually Say
plan.why: The myth-busting slot. It corrects beliefs already spreading ('no cure', 'airborne like COVID', 'extinct') in a save-and-share list. Every correction uses an agency's exact wording. | fact-check: The myth corrections are sound, but four fixes are needed. (1) Myth 4, 'only pneumonic spreads between people': quote CDC's droplet sentence exactly and credit it to CDC How Plague Spreads (updated May 15, 2024). Don't turn it into an absolute in our own voice, because WHO's fact sheet (updated Sep 29, 2026) notes rare person-to-person spread outside the pneumonic form, e.g. via infected material. Use 'Rare' plus WHO's wording if you include it. (2) Myth 3: say 'not airborne like measles' only via CDC's 'requires direct and close contact' and 'can sometimes cough droplets'. Keep 'sometimes' and the animal half. Don't say 'not contagious'. (3) The slide 1 status line must use WHO's Oct 10 DON wording, not 'WHO says the cause is still unclear; plague not confirmed' in our own voice. (4) Myth 5: credit preventive antibiotics to health authorities (WHO: 'seven-day chemoprophylaxis' for contacts), with no drug names or doses. Format note from the playbook: all 13 carousels reached 0–2 accounts, so the owner should consider rebuilding this as a Short. The topic itself is safe and approved with these fixes.

social.instagram_caption:
Plague: 6 myths vs CDC and WHO. As of Oct 10, 2026, WHO reports testing "did not identify plague or other tested high-threat pathogens" in the Irkutsk oblast laboratory worker who died, and no diagnosis has been confirmed.

WHO (Disease Outbreak News, Oct 10, 2026): medical observation has been completed for all identified contacts, with no additional cases. WHO adds: "A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker."

→ Myth: plague is extinct. CDC: in the US, "an average of five human plague cases have been reported each year" (range 0–17). That's human cases, not animal cases.
→ Myth: no cure. CDC: "Plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly."
→ Myth: airborne like COVID or measles. CDC: spread between people typically requires "direct and close contact". People and animals with plague pneumonia "can sometimes cough droplets".
→ Myth: all plague spreads between people. CDC: "Transmission of these droplets is the only way that plague can spread between people." WHO: human-to-human transmission of bubonic plague is rare.
→ Myth: home antibiotics will protect me. WHO: close contacts of pneumonic plague patients should be given "a seven-day chemoprophylaxis". That decision belongs to health professionals. Don't self-treat or stockpile antibiotics.
→ Myth: only rats spread plague. CDC: infected fleas, wild rodents and infected animals all play a part, and dogs and cats may bring plague-infected fleas into the home. Follow the label; some dog flea products (e.g. permethrin) are toxic to cats (PetMD).

Pneumonic plague signs on CDC's list: fever, cough, shortness of breath and chest pain. Possible exposure plus these signs? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.

Save this for the next plague rumor, and share it with someone who's heard "there's no cure."

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

slides.headline: Plague: 6 myths vs what CDC, WHO say
slides.body: Plague has been in the news this month. As of Oct 10, 2026, WHO reports that a laboratory worker in Irkutsk oblast died of pneumonia that media had reported as suspected pneumonic plague. WHO's risk assessment says 'testing did not identify plague or other tested high-threat pathogens', and that, according to authorities, the patient 'was determined to have died from pneumonia of undetermined etiology'. WHO: medical observation lasted seven days and has been completed for all identified contacts, with no additional cases. WHO adds: 'A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker.' (WHO Disease Outbreak News, Oct 10, 2026)
slides.bubble: Lots of rumors. Let's check them against the agencies.

slides.headline: Myth 3: airborne like COVID or measles
slides.body: CDC (How Plague Spreads): spread between people typically requires 'direct and close contact'. People and animals with plague pneumonia 'can sometimes cough droplets' containing plague bacteria.

factcheck.summary:
I checked every claim against the primary sources and they hold up. One quote on slide 2 needs a small wording fix.

WHO's Oct 10, 2026 Disease Outbreak News (DON620) contains all of the slide's quotes word for word:
- "testing did not identify plague or other tested high-threat pathogens"
- "was determined to have died from pneumonia of undetermined etiology"
- the seven days of medical observation, now completed for all identified contacts, with no additional cases
- "A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker."

A news search on Oct 12 turned up nothing newer than WHO's Oct 10 statement, so the status is current.

The CDC and WHO quotes on the other slides also match their sources word for word:
- "Plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly" (CDC About Plague, updated Aug 24, 2026).
- "direct and close contact", "can sometimes cough droplets", "the only way that plague can spread between people", dogs and cats bringing infected fleas into the home, and handling tissue or body fluids (CDC How Plague Spreads, updated May 15, 2024).
- Fever, headache, weakness, shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, and sometimes bloody or watery mucus (CDC Signs and Symptoms of Plague).
- Flea control for pets (CDC Preventing Plague, updated Mar 5, 2025).
- "Human-to-human transmission of bubonic plague is rare" and "a seven-day chemoprophylaxis" for close contacts (WHO fact sheet, updated Sep 29, 2026).
- The permethrin warning and the advice to follow the label (PetMD, updated Apr 8, 2025).

The safety lines are all in place: the urgent-contact line, the "don't self-treat or stockpile antibiotics" line, the cat-safety caveat and "If you're worried, talk to a health professional." The title fits our rules and the slides deliver what it promises.

The fix: slide 2 quotes CDC as saying cases "are reported" each year, but the Plague Maps and Statistics page (updated Oct 7, 2026) says "have been reported". Because the slide uses quote marks, the wording has to match exactly.
